## Introduction

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are effective for treating depression, though safety concerns often limit their use. Common adverse effects of TCAs include anticholinergic symptoms, orthostatic hypotension, sedation, and cardiotoxicity, particularly in overdose. Major depressive disorder is an indication for TCA administration when selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are ineffective, not tolerated, or contraindicated. Additional indications include neuropathic and chronic pain conditions and sleep disorders, including chronic insomnia refractory to other agents.[1] TCAs are also prescribed for obsessive-compulsive disorder when 1st-line treatments fail, as well as for enuresis in children. Antidepressants were among the most commonly reported substance classes to US Poison Centers in 2022 and 2023, and TCA exposures were associated with more serious outcomes than other antidepressant exposures.[2]

## Etiology

TCAs are associated with severe toxicity because of their narrow therapeutic index, activity at multiple receptors, and frequent prescription to patients with conditions that increase the risk of suicide by overdose. Intentional self-harm is the leading cause of TCA overdose in adults. In children, accidental or exploratory ingestions can cause significant toxicity because of the narrow therapeutic index of these drugs.

## Pathophysiology

The therapeutic effect of TCAs in depression results from norepinephrine inhibition and serotonin reuptake within the central nervous system (CNS). However, TCAs exert 7 distinct pharmacologic actions that contribute to adverse effects and toxicity, as follows:

α1-Adrenergic receptor inhibition: Causes vasodilation, hypotension, and reflex tachycardia

Histamine receptor inhibition: Produces sedation, altered mental status, and increased seizure risk

Muscarinic receptor inhibition: Leads to antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) effects, including tachycardia, mydriasis, urinary retention, decreased bowel sounds, dry skin, and delirium

Cardiac sodium channel inhibition: Slows phase 0 of the cardiac action potential, prolonging the QRS interval and increasing the risk of hypotension and dysrhythmias

Cardiac potassium efflux channel inhibition: Slows phase 3 of the cardiac action potential, prolonging the QT interval and increasing the risk of torsades de pointes

γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) type A receptor antagonism: Reduces chloride conductance, causing neuroexcitation and seizures

Biogenic amine reuptake inhibition: Contributes to CNS and autonomic nervous system effects, including seizures

Overall, TCA toxicity results from the combined CNS, antimuscarinic, and cardiotoxic effects of these mechanisms. Severe overdose can be life-threatening.

## Toxicokinetics

TCAs are rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and exhibit high bioavailability. TCA poisoning produces anticholinergic effects that slow gastrointestinal motility, delaying absorption and peak drug concentrations. Coingestion of other agents with anticholinergic properties, such as antiparkinsonian medications and 1st-generation antihistamines, further contributes to unpredictable absorption. TCAs are highly lipid-soluble and extensively protein-bound. Most TCAs undergo substantial 1st-pass hepatic metabolism, primarily through cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6), before renal elimination. TCAs are often formulated as immediate-release products with relatively short elimination half-lives, although coingestion of cytochrome P450 2D6 inducers or inhibitors can alter TCA metabolism.[6] Toxicity results from both the parent drug and active metabolites. Respiratory or metabolic acidosis increases the free, pharmacologically active TCA fraction, enhancing toxicity.

The manifestations of toxicity usually become apparent within 2 hours of ingestion. Patients without signs or symptoms 6 hours after ingestion are unlikely to have sustained a clinically significant overdose and may be medically cleared for subsequent psychiatric care after this observation period. Toxicity usually lasts 24 to 48 hours but is highly dose-dependent.[7]

## History and Physical

When TCA toxicity is suspected, the history should include the specific drug ingested, estimated dose, formulation, time of ingestion, and any coingestants, including prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal products. Past medical history should document cardiac disease, seizure disorders, and psychiatric conditions. Initial symptoms commonly include CNS manifestations, such as agitation, confusion, delirium, drowsiness, and seizures, as well as autonomic findings, including dry mouth and urinary retention.

Physical examination may reveal tachycardia, hypotension, and, in severe cases, hyperthermia. Physical findings may also include flushed, dry skin, mydriasis, and decreased bowel sounds. Neurologic examination may demonstrate CNS depression, delirium, ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, or seizures. Cardiovascular evaluation often detects conduction abnormalities, including QRS and QT interval prolongation, with increasing interval duration associated with a greater risk of arrhythmias. Overall, these findings reflect the anticholinergic, cardiotoxic, and CNS effects of TCA toxicity. Careful monitoring is essential for effective management.
